comparisons.interpretation: Uyterhoeven supports a Massachusetts single-payer system; Sharp explicitly answers no to that state-level proposal while supporting federal single payer. The disagreement must not be generalized into Sharp opposing single payer at every level.

Uyterhoeven foregrounds rent-control authority and public investment; Sharp foregrounds housing supply and transit-oriented development. Both also support tenant protections and transit-area multifamily housing, so these are not mutually exclusive platforms.
Uyterhoeven emphasizes grassroots accountability and changing who state government serves; Sharp emphasizes internal cultural reform, shared understandings and program evaluation.
Both explicitly support Massachusetts single payer. Barber's additional public-option proposal is described as a step toward it, not a repudiation of it.

Callahan emphasizes organizing a statewide single-payer movement; Barber names a MassHealth buy-in public option as an interim route. Callahan also says she accepts useful incremental bills, so this is not an uncompromising-versus-pragmatic binary.

Callahan foregrounds social housing and land trusts; Barber foregrounds zoning, accessibility and tenant protections. Both support tenant protections and housing production; omission is not opposition.
Callahan makes movement-building her leading governing strategy; Barber emphasizes legislative and advocacy coalitions that can pass policy. Both describe working with groups beyond the legislature.
Saval proposes rent stabilization directly; Farnese favors considering rent control after public debate and design work. The latter is a qualified deliberative position, not explicit opposition.
Both support community land trusts, with Saval specifying public acquisition and restricted-affordability transfers and Farnese proposing growth incentives.

Saval endorses a fracking ban linked to worker-transition programs. Farnese supports a ban at least during review of permitting. The difference is its stated duration and conditions, not a simple pro-/anti-ban split.

Both support supervised consumption sites; Farnese explicitly requires host-community support before operation. Saval's answer does not state that condition, but its absence is not proof he rejects community consultation.
Both support an AB5-style worker-classification law. Saval discusses negotiating clearer exemptions; Farnese says implementation is under review.
Saval specifies a $15 floor; Farnese gives a $12-15 range with inflation indexing. An exact Farnese endpoint or categorical rejection of $15 is not invented.
Saval emphasizes movement representation; Farnese emphasizes cross-party relationships and electing a Democratic majority. These are stated approaches, not measured effectiveness.
